mcqs.question: What does URLSearchParams.getAll('tag') provide?
options: Only the last tag value
All values associated with tag
A parsed number for tag
The full URL including its origin
mcqs.explanation: getAll returns every value for a repeated key. get returns only the first, and URLSearchParams works with query parameters rather than parsing a full URL string as a URL object.

mcqs.question: Why stabilize a Jotai atom created from component input?
options: Atom configs hold values only in local variables
Atom identity is referential and a new definition can be made every render
Stable atoms disable dependency tracking
Jotai requires all atoms to be global constants
mcqs.explanation: An atom config is an immutable definition whose identity matters. useMemo or useRef provides stable identity for a dynamic definition; dependency tracking still works through get.

mcqs.question: Which value is usually the best state for a selected item when the item data already lives in an array?
options: A duplicated selected item object
The selected item's rendered HTML
The selected item ID
A second server cache
mcqs.explanation: Storing the ID avoids duplicating the entity. The selected object can be derived from the current array, so edits remain consistent.

mcqs.question: Where should a short-lived form draft normally live?
options: In the server cache on every keypress
In the form boundary
Only in the URL, including secrets
In every component that displays the resource
mcqs.explanation: Draft, dirty, validation, and submission state belong to the form workflow. The server cache represents persisted data and should be reconciled after submit.

mcqs.question: A search box must show only the latest query's results. Which operator makes that the default behavior?
options: switchMap: it cancels the previous inner request when a new one starts
concatMap: it queues queries and runs them in order
exhaustMap: it ignores new queries while one is in flight
mergeMap: it runs every query concurrently
mcqs.explanation: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner observable, so only the latest query can update the UI. concatMap preserves order but lets stale results arrive late; exhaustMap drops queries; mergeMap interleaves them.

mcqs.question: What does a memoized selector give you in NgRx?
options: Derived views recomputed only when their input slice of state changes
Mutable state that components can write to directly
Automatic HTTP caching for effects
Time-travel debugging by itself
mcqs.explanation: Selectors derive read views from the store and memoize on their inputs, so components recompute only when the state they depend on changes. The store stays immutable and owned by reducers.

mcqs.question: A preferences object is read by three components on different routes, changes only when the user edits settings, and has no complex update coordination. Following the state-scope decision in the bank, who should own it?
options: A global store, because more than one component reads the value
Local state in each of the three components, kept in sync with an effect
Context from the closest common provider: readers are distant, but updates are simple and infrequent
A global store when the data comes from the server, and Context otherwise
mcqs.explanation: Distance decides whether sharing is needed, not how much machinery to add. Context already removes prop drilling for a subtree, and with simple, infrequent updates there is no coordination or inspection payoff that would justify a store (https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context). The strongest distractor is 'a global store because more than one component reads it': it equates shared with global, but two readers are handled by one provider, while a store earns its place when updates are frequent or complex, many writers must agree, or state must be inspected consistently over time (https://redux.js.org/faq/general). The last option confuses ownership with placement: server-owned data belongs in the server-state cache whichever container the client state uses.

mcqs.question: An `AuthProvider` renders `<AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, login }}>` where `login` is recreated on every render and `user` is unchanged. Its parent re-renders for an unrelated reason. What happens below the provider?
options: Nothing re-renders, because `user` is the same object and React compares context values field by field
Only the direct children re-render; deeper consumers are shielded once they are wrapped in `memo`
Consumers re-render only if they also receive changed props alongside the context read
Every component that reads `AuthContext` below the provider re-renders, including ones wrapped in `memo`
mcqs.explanation: Context compares the whole `value` by `Object.is`, and an inline object literal has a new identity on every provider render, so consumers receive a new value even though `user` is unchanged. A context subscription lives on the consumer, and `memo` cannot block it because the update does not arrive as a prop (https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext). The strongest distractor is the field-by-field comparison: it sounds like React does structural equality, but a single reference comparison is exactly why the inline object is the classic accidental trigger; `useMemo` over `[user, login]` plus `useCallback` for `login` is the fix. The neighbouring distractor is the related but wrong belief that `memo` protects consumers, when it only protects the props path.

mcqs.question: A theme toggle must survive reloads and the page is server-rendered. Which sequence keeps hydration correct?
options: `useState(() => localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light')` so the first client render already shows the saved theme
Render a fixed default first, read `localStorage` in an effect after mount, then update; if the value must be right on first paint, serialize it into the server output
Branch on `typeof window` during render: the server returns the default and the client reads storage
Read the theme from a module-level variable during render so the server and the client share the same value
mcqs.explanation: Hydration attaches React to server HTML and requires the first client render to produce the same output the server produced. `localStorage` is browser-only, so a fixed default is rendered first, the effect reads storage after hydration, and the update lands in a normal re-render; when the persisted value cannot wait, the server must serialize the same snapshot so both sides agree from the start (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot). The strongest distractor is the lazy initializer: it is the idiomatic read-once pattern in a client-only app and even saves one render, but during hydration it makes the client's first render differ from the server markup, which is precisely the mismatch this question is about. The `typeof window` branch creates two different trees, and a module-level variable is per-process state that does not exist as a shared snapshot between server and client.

scenarios.prompt: A settings form is open while another tab updates the same profile. A refetch arrives after the user edits only the display name. Propose a safe state and reconciliation policy.

code.caption: Blindly reseeding draft state from every server update can erase edits.

scenarios.modelAnswer: Do not overwrite the whole draft whenever `profile` changes. Keep the persisted server snapshot and the workflow draft as separate concepts, track dirty fields, and seed only on the form's initial load or an intentional reset. When a new profile arrives, merge server values into untouched fields while preserving the edited displayName, or surface a conflict if the same field changed remotely. Submit a command with a version or other concurrency token when lost updates matter. On success, treat the authoritative response as the new baseline, then reconcile or invalidate the relevant query.
rubric: Identifies the effect as destructive for dirty fields.
Separates server baseline from draft and tracks dirty fields or an equivalent policy.
Defines behavior for untouched versus concurrently changed fields.
Uses a version or conflict path when lost updates matter.
Resets the baseline from the authoritative mutation response or deliberate refetch.

scenarios.prompt: The app mounts once, then the user clicks the theme button inside `Sidebar`. Predict exactly which `render …` lines appear on the first mount and again after that single click, explain why `memo` does not save `UserBadge`, and refactor the providers so a theme change no longer re-renders session consumers.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Prediction. On the first mount every component mounts once: `render AppProviders`, `render Sidebar`, `render UserBadge`, `render Footer`. After the single click the log shows `render AppProviders`, `render Sidebar`, `render UserBadge` — no `render Footer`.

Why the click reaches so far. `theme` lives in `AppProviders`, so `setTheme` re-renders that component. Both provider elements receive inline object literals, so on that render each `value` is a fresh object. Context compares values by `Object.is`, not field by field, so the `SessionContext` value also looks new even though `session` itself did not change. `Sidebar` is a legitimate consumer of `ThemeContext`, and `UserBadge` is a consumer of a value that changed identity, so both re-render. `memo` is irrelevant here: it memoizes props, while a context consumer must re-render to receive the new value; that is also why wrapping consumers in `memo` is the classic failed fix. `Footer` reads no context, and its element arrives through the stable `children` prop of a parent that did not re-render, so `memo` bails out. Note the two distinct events people conflate: the provider component re-rendering (cheap) and its consumers re-rendering (what the log shows).

Refactor. First colocate the state: give the theme its own `ThemeProvider` that owns `useState`, and keep `SessionProvider` separate, so a theme update never renders the component that holds the session. Second, stabilize what each provider hands down: `const signOut = useCallback(() => setSession(null), [])` and `const sessionValue = useMemo(() => ({ session, signOut }), [session, signOut])`; likewise for `toggle` and the theme value. With stable values, even a re-render of the provider for an unrelated reason leaves the other context value identical and its consumers untouched. Third, keep each provider as close as possible to the subtree that reads it. If consumers ever need narrower subscriptions than one value per context, that is the point to reach for an external store with selectors instead of splitting contexts indefinitely.
rubric: Predicts the first mount as all four components, and the post-click log as AppProviders, Sidebar and UserBadge with Footer absent
Explains that inline object literals get a new identity under Object.is, so the session value changes even though `session` did not
States that memo does not block context updates for consumers — it only covers the props path — which is why UserBadge re-renders
Refactors by colocating theme state in its own provider and/or memoizing each provided value and its callbacks with useMemo/useCallback
Separates provider re-render from consumer re-render, and names narrow subscriptions or provider placement as the durable fix, not more memo
